fields.title: Python Programming
fields.description:
Python Programming is a structured introduction to programming that develops
both computational reasoning and practical software-development ability. The
course begins with Python syntax and fundamental programming concepts before
progressively exploring variables and data types, input and output, decision
making, iteration, functions, collections, file handling, modules, and
object-oriented programming.

Throughout the curriculum, learners are encouraged to move beyond memorising
syntax and instead develop the ability to analyse problems, decompose
requirements, design algorithms, write readable code, interpret errors, and
refine solutions through deliberate testing. Practical exercises connect
abstract concepts to realistic programming tasks so that theoretical knowledge
is repeatedly converted into demonstrable competence.

By the conclusion of the course, learners should be able to design and
implement small Python programs with confidence, explain the reasoning behind
their solutions, troubleshoot common programming errors, work effectively
with Python's core data structures, and apply object-oriented thinking to
larger programs. The course also provides the conceptual foundation required
for subsequent study of Django, automation, backend engineering, data
processing, and other areas of professional software development.

fields.title: Django Web Development
fields.description:
Django Web Development provides a structured pathway from Python web
programming fundamentals to the design of complete, maintainable,
database-backed web applications. The course introduces Django's architecture
and project structure before progressing through URL routing, views, templates,
static assets, models, database interaction, forms, authentication,
authorization, administrative workflows, testing, security, and deployment
considerations.

The curriculum emphasises the relationship between the different layers of a
web application rather than presenting Django as a collection of unrelated
features. Learners examine how HTTP requests move through URL configuration
into application logic, how models and the ORM represent persistent data, how
templates present information, and how authentication and authorization
protect user and application resources.

Practical work is framed around realistic web-application scenarios so that
learners can develop sound engineering judgement alongside framework
knowledge. By the end of the course, learners should be able to structure a
Django project coherently, design database-backed features, process validated
user input, implement secure authentication and authorization, use the
administrative interface responsibly, test application behaviour, and prepare
a Django application for dependable deployment.

fields.title: Django REST Framework
fields.description:
Django REST Framework (DRF) is a powerful toolkit for designing, implementing,
testing, and securing web APIs with Django. This course develops a systematic
understanding of API engineering, beginning with HTTP communication, RESTful
principles, resources, endpoints, and request-response semantics before
progressing to project configuration, serialization, validation, API views,
generic views, ViewSets, routers, authentication, authorization, automated
testing, observability, and production readiness.

The curriculum combines conceptual reasoning with practical implementation.
Learners examine how frontend clients communicate with backend services, how
data crosses application boundaries, how API contracts are structured, how
incoming information is validated, and how security policies protect
sensitive resources. Particular attention is given to the rationale behind
technical decisions, enabling learners to understand not only how a feature
works, but also when and why it should be used.

Practical activities are grounded in realistic technology-platform scenarios,
including course catalogues, learner progress, submissions, authentication,
permissions, and instructor workflows. By the end of the course, learners
should be able to design coherent RESTful interfaces, construct validated API
endpoints, choose appropriate DRF abstractions, enforce server-side security
rules, test both expected and failure conditions, and evaluate an API for
production readiness.

The course provides a strong foundation for backend engineering, full-stack
development, API-driven systems, distributed applications, and further study
of professional software architecture.

fields.title: Python Fundamentals
fields.description:
This module establishes a rigorous foundation in Python programming and
computational problem solving. The sequence begins with the language itself
and progressively develops the learner's ability to represent information,
receive and produce data, make decisions, repeat operations, organise logic
into reusable functions, manage collections, and model more complex behaviour
through object-oriented programming.

The emphasis throughout is on understanding why a programming technique is
useful, how it behaves, and when it should be preferred over an alternative.
Learners are expected to develop readable, testable, and logically structured
solutions rather than simply reproduce isolated examples.

fields.title: Django Fundamentals
fields.description:
This module introduces the architecture and principal building blocks of a
Django web application. Learners progress from project organisation and URL
routing into views, templates, static assets, models, database interaction,
forms, authentication, authorization, and administrative management.

The sequence is designed to show how these components cooperate within one
web application. Rather than studying each feature in isolation, learners
develop an understanding of the complete request-response lifecycle and the
design decisions that make a Django application understandable, secure,
maintainable, and extensible.

fields.title: DRF Fundamentals
fields.description:
This module establishes the conceptual and practical foundations required to
engineer dependable APIs with Django REST Framework. The sequence progresses
from HTTP and REST principles through project configuration, serialization and
validation, function-based and class-based views, generic abstractions,
ViewSets and routers, authentication and authorization, automated testing,
observability, and production practices.

The objective is not simply to memorise framework syntax. Learners are
expected to reason about resource boundaries, API contracts, data integrity,
security, maintainability, testing strategy, and operational reliability.
Each lesson adds another layer to that engineering perspective, allowing
individual DRF features to be understood as parts of a coherent backend
architecture.

fields.title: Introduction to Python
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This opening lesson establishes the intellectual foundation for programming with Python. Learners are introduced to Python as a readable, expressive language and begin connecting syntax with computational thinking, program structure, and practical software development.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on understanding the role of Python beyond simple examples: a language used for automation, backend development, data processing, testing, and rapid application development.

Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language known for its simple syntax and readability. In this lesson, we introduce Python, its uses, installation, and the basic structure of a Python program.

fields.title: Variables and Data Types
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops a precise understanding of how Python represents and manipulates information. Learners examine variables, primitive data types, assignment, conversion, and the relationship between a value and the name used to reference it.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on choosing appropriate representations for data and writing code whose intent remains clear to other developers.

Variables are used to store data in Python. Python supports several basic data types including integers, floating-point numbers, strings, and Boolean values. In this lesson, we learn how to create variables and work with different data types.

fields.title: Input and Output
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson introduces the interaction between a Python program and the person or system supplying its input. Learners examine how information is received, transformed, validated, and presented as meaningful output.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on designing predictable input-output behaviour and recognising that real programs must account for different kinds of user input.

Python provides the input() function for receiving information from the user and the print() function for displaying information. This lesson introduces basic input and output operations.

fields.title: Conditional Statements
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops the reasoning patterns required for decision-making in software. Learners use conditional logic to translate requirements and logical conditions into explicit program behaviour.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on expressing business rules clearly and constructing branches that remain readable as requirements become more sophisticated.

Conditional statements allow a Python program to make decisions. We will learn how to use if, elif, and else to execute different blocks of code depending on conditions.

fields.title: Loops
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson introduces iteration as a fundamental mechanism for processing repeated work efficiently. Learners compare for and while loops, examine loop conditions, and consider how iteration interacts with decisions and data structures.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on designing repetition that is both correct and bounded, while avoiding unnecessary duplication or uncontrolled execution.

Loops allow a Python program to repeat a block of code efficiently. Python mainly provides two looping structures: 1. for loops 2. while loops A for loop is useful when you want to iterate over a sequence or repeat an operation a known number of times. Example: for number in range(1, 6): print(number) This prints the numbers 1 through 5. The range() function is commonly used with for loops. For example: for number in range(5): print(number) prints: 0 1 2 3 4 A while loop repeats code while a condition remains true. Example: count = 1 while count <= 5: print(count) count += 1 The loop stops when the condition becomes false. A loop can also contain an if statement. This allows a program to make decisions during repetition. Example: for number in range(1, 11): if number % 2 == 0: print(number) This prints the even numbers from 1 to 10. Important ideas to remember: - for loops are commonly used to iterate over sequences or ranges. - while loops continue while a condition is true. - range() is useful for generating a sequence of numbers. - A loop variable changes as the loop progresses. - A while loop must eventually change its condition or it may run forever. - Loops can be combined with conditional statements. Try to predict the output of loop examples before running them. Then modify the examples and observe how the output changes.

fields.title: Functions
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson introduces functions as a means of organising behaviour into reusable and understandable units. Learners explore parameters, arguments, return values, default values, and the relationship between a function's inputs and outputs.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on writing functions with clear responsibilities so that programs become easier to test, reuse, maintain, and extend.

Functions allow you to organize reusable pieces of Python code. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, you can place it inside a function and call the function whenever you need it. A simple function looks like this: def greet(): print("Hello, Python!") You call the function by using its name followed by parentheses: greet() A function can accept parameters. Parameters allow you to provide data to the function. Example: def greet(name): print("Hello,", name) greet("Victor") A function can also return a value. Example: def add(a, b): return a + b result = add(5, 3) print(result) The return statement sends a value back to the code that called the function. Functions can have multiple parameters: def calculate_total(price, quantity): return price * quantity total = calculate_total(100, 3) print(total) Python also allows default parameter values: def greet(name="Student"): print("Hello,", name) greet() greet("Victor") Important ideas to remember: - def is used to define a function. - A function can accept zero or more parameters. - Arguments are the actual values passed to a function. - return sends a result back to the caller. - Functions help reduce duplicated code. - Functions make programs easier to organize, test, and maintain. When designing a function, think about: 1. What information does the function need? 2. What should the function do? 3. What result should it return? Good functions usually have a clear purpose and a descriptive name.

fields.title: Collections
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops fluency with Python's principal built-in collection types: lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries. Learners compare their behaviour and consider how the choice of data structure affects the way information is organised and accessed.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on selecting a collection according to the requirements of the problem rather than treating all collections as interchangeable.

Python collections allow you to store and organize multiple values in a single variable. The main built-in collection types covered in this lesson are: 1. Lists 2. Tuples 3. Sets 4. Dictionaries LISTS A list is an ordered, changeable collection. Example: fruits = ["apple", "banana", "orange"] You can access a list item using its index: print(fruits[0]) This prints: apple List indexes start at 0. Lists can be changed after they are created: fruits[1] = "mango" You can add an item with append(): fruits. append("grape") You can remove an item with remove(): fruits. remove("apple") You can loop through a list: for fruit in fruits: print(fruit) TUPLES A tuple is an ordered collection that cannot normally be changed after it has been created. Example: coordinates = (10, 20) You can access tuple items using indexes: print(coordinates[0]) Tuples are useful when you want a fixed collection of values. SETS A set is an unordered collection of unique values. Example: numbers = {1, 2, 3, 3} The duplicate 3 is stored only once. You can add an item: numbers. add(4) Sets are useful when you need to work with unique values. DICTIONARIES A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Example: student = { "name": "Student", "age": 20, "course": "Python" } You can access a value using its key: print(student["name"]) You can add or update values: student["age"] = 21 student["level"] = "Beginner" You can loop through a dictionary: for key, value in student. items(): print(key, value) CHOOSING A COLLECTION Use a list when: - order matters; - values may need to change; - duplicate values are allowed. Use a tuple when: - order matters; - the collection should remain fixed. Use a set when: - unique values are required; - duplicate values should be removed. Use a dictionary when: - information naturally belongs to named keys; - you need key-value pairs. Important ideas to remember: - List indexes begin at 0. - Lists are mutable. - Tuples are generally immutable. - Sets contain unique values. - Dictionaries store key-value pairs. - Collections can be combined with loops and conditional statements. Practice accessing, changing, and iterating over collections so that these structures become comfortable to use in larger Python programs.

fields.title: Object-Oriented Programming
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson introduces object-oriented programming and the use of classes and objects to combine related data and behaviour. Learners examine attributes, constructors, methods, and the relationship between a class and the objects created from it.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on modelling larger software systems in a way that groups related responsibilities and supports maintainable application architecture.

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming approach that organizes code around objects and the data and behavior associated with those objects. In Python, OOP is built around classes and objects. CLASSES A class is a blueprint for creating objects. Example: class Student: pass This defines a class called Student. OBJECTS An object is an instance created from a class. Example: student1 = Student() student2 = Student() student1 and student2 are separate objects created from the Student class. ATTRIBUTES Attributes store data belonging to an object. Example: class Student: pass student = Student() student. name = "Student" student. age = 20 print(student. name) print(student. age) CONSTRUCTORS The __init__() method is commonly used to initialize object attributes. Example: class Student: def __init__(self, name, age): self. name = name self. age = age student = Student("Student", 20) print(student. name) print(student. age) The self parameter refers to the current object. METHODS Methods are functions defined inside a class. Example: class Student: def __init__(self, name): self. name = name def greet(self): print("Hello,", self. name) student = Student("Student") student. greet() METHODS CAN RETURN VALUES A method can also return a result. Example: class Calculator: def add(self, a, b): return a + b calculator = Calculator() result = calculator. add(5, 3) print(result) The result is: 8 WHY USE OOP? Object-oriented programming can help you: - organize larger programs; - group related data and behavior; - reuse code; - represent real-world concepts in software; - make programs easier to maintain. CLASSES AND REAL-WORLD CONCEPTS For example, a school system could contain a Student class: class Student: def __init__(self, name, course): self. name = name self. course = course def introduce(self): print("I am", self. name) print("I am studying", self. course) student = Student("Student", "Python") student. introduce() A single class can therefore describe many similar objects. IMPORTANT OOP CONCEPTS Class: A blueprint used to create objects. Object: An instance of a class. Attribute: Data stored on an object. Method: A function belonging to a class. Constructor: The __init__() method commonly used to initialize an object. self: A reference to the current object. As you progress beyond basic Python, object-oriented programming becomes especially useful for designing larger applications and frameworks. Django itself makes extensive use of Python classes and objects, so a good understanding of OOP will help you understand Django models, views, forms, serializers, and other components later in this course.

fields.title: Introduction to Django
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson establishes a conceptual foundation for Django by examining why web frameworks exist and how Django organises the major components of a web application. Learners encounter the request-response lifecycle, projects, applications, models, templates, and views.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on understanding Django as an architectural framework rather than merely a collection of commands and files.

Django is a high-level Python web framework used to build web applications. Django provides many features that help developers build applications more quickly and consistently, including URL routing, templates, forms, authentication, database integration, and an administrative interface. WHY DJANGO? A web application normally needs several connected parts: - URLs that identify pages and resources. - Views that contain application logic. - Templates that generate HTML. - Models that represent stored data. - A database for persistent information. Django provides a structured way to organize these components. PROJECTS AND APPS A Django project is the overall configuration and deployment structure for a website or web application. A Django project can contain multiple applications. A Django application is a Python package focused on a particular area of functionality. For example, a learning platform might contain: - accounts - academy - payments - notifications PROJECT STRUCTURE A typical Django project contains files and directories such as: manage. py project configuration package application packages templates static files The manage. py file provides a command-line entry point for common Django administration tasks. The project configuration package commonly contains: - settings. py - urls. py - asgi. py - wsgi. py settings. py contains project configuration. urls. py defines URL routing. asgi. py and wsgi. py provide interfaces used to run Django through different server environments. DJANGO APPLICATIONS Applications contain functionality for a particular domain. A typical Django application may contain: models. py views. py urls. py admin. py tests. py models. py defines database-backed data structures. views. py contains request-handling logic. urls. py connects URL patterns to views. admin. py configures the Django admin interface. tests. py contains automated tests. THE REQUEST-RESPONSE FLOW A simplified Django request flow is: Browser ? URL ? View ? Model / database (when needed) ? Template (when needed) ? HTTP response ? Browser For example, a student visiting a course page sends an HTTP request to Django. Django matches the URL, calls the appropriate view, obtains the required data, renders a template, and returns the response. DJANGO'S MTV PATTERN Django commonly describes its architecture using: Model Template View Model: Represents application data and database interaction. Template: Controls how information is presented to the user. View: Processes requests and coordinates application logic. The URL configuration connects incoming URLs to the appropriate views. DJANGO AND PYTHON Django is built with Python, so Python fundamentals are important before working deeply with Django. The Python concepts you have already studied are particularly useful for: - variables; - functions; - collections; - classes and objects; - modules; - exceptions. Django makes extensive use of Python classes and objects, so the previous Object-Oriented Programming lesson provides an important foundation. DEVELOPMENT WORKFLOW A typical Django development workflow is: 1. Create a project. 2. Create one or more applications. 3. Configure installed applications. 4. Define models. 5. Create and apply migrations. 6. Define views. 7. Configure URLs. 8. Create templates. 9. Test the application. 10. Run and deploy the application. As you progress through this course, you will build these pieces incrementally and connect them into a working web application.

fields.title: Django Project Setup and Structure
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops practical understanding of Django project creation, configuration, application registration, migrations, URL configuration, and the command-line workflow used throughout development.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on establishing disciplined project structure so that future features can be developed without creating unnecessary architectural confusion.

A Django project provides the overall configuration for a web application. After learning what Django is, the next step is understanding how a Django project is created, organized, configured, and prepared for development. CREATING A DJANGO PROJECT A new Django project can be created from the command line with: django-admin startproject myproject This creates a project directory containing Django's initial configuration. The project commonly contains: manage. py myproject/ __init__. py settings. py urls. py asgi. py wsgi. py MANAGE. PY manage. py is a command-line utility associated with a Django project. Common commands include: python manage. py runserver python manage. py check python manage. py makemigrations python manage. py migrate python manage. py createsuperuser RUNSERVER The development server can be started with: python manage. py runserver Django normally starts a local development server that can be accessed from a browser. SETTINGS. PY The settings. py file contains configuration for the Django project. Important settings include: INSTALLED_APPS MIDDLEWARE ROOT_URLCONF TEMPLATES DATABASES STATIC_URL DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD INSTALLED_APPS Django applications must normally be registered in INSTALLED_APPS before their models, templates, or other components are used as part of the project. For example: INSTALLED_APPS = [ ... "academy", ] URL CONFIGURATION The urls. py file defines URL routing for the project. A URL pattern connects a URL path to a view. For example: from django. urls import path from . views import home urlpatterns = [ path("", home), ] In larger projects, application-specific URL configurations can be included from the main project URL configuration. CREATING AN APPLICATION A Django application can be created with: python manage. py startapp academy This creates an application directory containing files such as: admin. py apps. py models. py tests. py views. py Additional files such as urls. py can be created as needed. PROJECTS VS APPLICATIONS A project is the overall configuration of the Django website or system. An application is a focused component that provides a particular area of functionality. For example, a learning platform might have: project configuration ??? accounts application ??? academy application ??? notifications application MIGRATIONS Django uses migrations to manage changes to database-backed models. After changing a model, developers commonly run: python manage. py makemigrations This creates migration instructions. The changes can then be applied to the database using: python manage. py migrate Migrations allow database structure to evolve in a controlled way while the application changes over time. CHECKING A PROJECT Django provides a system check command: python manage. py check This can detect configuration and application issues before deployment. DEVELOPMENT ORDER A useful beginner workflow is: 1. Create the Django project. 2. Create an application. 3. Register the application. 4. Define models. 5. Create migrations. 6. Apply migrations. 7. Create views. 8. Configure URLs. 9. Create templates. 10. Run and test the application. The project structure provides the foundation for everything you will build later in this course. As the Django course progresses, each lesson will build another part of this foundation until you can create a complete Django web application.

fields.title: URL Routing and Views
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson explains how Django translates incoming URLs into application behaviour. Learners explore URL patterns, views, parameters, named routes, includes, redirects, and the distinction between retrieving information and submitting state changes.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on designing predictable URL structures and maintaining a clean separation between routing and business logic.

Django uses URL routing to decide which part of the application should handle an incoming web request. A URL pattern connects a URL path to a view. The basic flow is: Browser ? URL ? URL pattern ? View ? Response ? Browser URLCONF Django stores URL patterns in URL configuration files, commonly named urls. py. A simple URL configuration looks like this: from django. urls import path from . import views urlpatterns = [ path("", views. home, name="home"), ] The path() function connects a URL pattern to a view. VIEWS A Django view is Python code that receives a request and returns a response. A simple view can return an HttpResponse: from django. http import HttpResponse def home(request): return HttpResponse("Hello, Django!") When a user visits the URL connected to this view, Django returns the text "Hello, Django!". FUNCTION-BASED VIEWS The example above is called a function-based view because the view is implemented as a Python function. A function-based view normally accepts a request parameter: def home(request): return HttpResponse("Welcome to my site") The request object contains information about the incoming HTTP request. RENDERING TEMPLATES Most web pages need HTML rather than plain text. Django provides the render() shortcut for returning an HTML template. Example: from django. shortcuts import render def home(request): return render(request, "home. html") The template file can contain HTML:

Welcome to Django

PASSING DATA TO TEMPLATES Views can send data to templates using a context dictionary. Example: def profile(request): context = { "name": "Student", "course": "Django", } return render( request, "profile. html", context, ) The template can access these values:

{{ name }}

{{ course }}

URL PARAMETERS URLs can contain parameters. For example: path("courses//", views. course_detail) If a user visits: /courses/5/ Django passes the value 5 to the view. The view can receive it: def course_detail(request, course_id): return HttpResponse( f"Course ID: {course_id}" ) STRING PARAMETERS Django can also capture text values. Example: path("courses//", views. course_detail) A URL such as: /courses/python-programming/ can pass the slug into the view. NAMED URLS URL patterns can have names: path( "courses//", views. course_detail, name="course_detail", ) Named URLs make it easier to generate links without hard-coding URLs. In templates, Django can generate a URL with: {% url "course_detail" slug=course. slug %} URL INCLUDES Larger applications often keep application-specific URLs in the application itself. The main project urls. py can include those URLs. Example: from django. urls import include, path urlpatterns = [ path("courses/", include("academy. urls")), ] This allows the academy application to maintain its own URL patterns. HTTP METHODS Views can handle different HTTP methods. A request can use methods such as: GET POST PUT PATCH DELETE HTML forms commonly use GET or POST. A view can inspect the request method: if request. method == "POST": # process submitted data ... HTTP RESPONSE TYPES A Django view can return: - HttpResponse; - rendered templates; - redirects; - JSON responses. For example: from django. shortcuts import redirect return redirect("home") The redirect tells the browser to request another URL. GET VS POST GET requests are commonly used to retrieve information. POST requests are commonly used to submit data that may change application state. For example, a course page may use GET to display information, while a submission form may use POST to send a student's work to Django. URL ROUTING AND APPLICATION DESIGN Good URL structures make an application easier to understand. For example: /courses/ /courses/python-programming/ /courses/python-programming/lessons/1/ /courses/python-programming/progress/ The URL communicates what resource the user is accessing. KEY IDEAS Remember: - urls. py defines URL patterns. - path() connects paths to views. - A view processes a request and returns a response. - render() can return an HTML template. - Context data allows views to send information to templates. - URL parameters allow dynamic URLs. - Named URLs make URL generation safer and easier to maintain. - include() allows application-specific URL configurations. - GET and POST are commonly used for different types of requests. Understanding URL routing and views is essential because they connect the browser-facing part of a Django application to its Python application logic.

fields.title: Templates and Static Files
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson examines Django's presentation layer through templates, context data, template tags, inheritance, static assets, and form rendering. Learners consider how HTML is generated without moving core application logic into templates.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on creating maintainable presentation layers that communicate clearly with backend application logic.

Django templates are used to generate the HTML that is sent to a browser. Templates allow you to separate the presentation of a web page from the Python logic that processes requests. A typical Django flow is: Browser ? URL ? View ? Template ? HTML response ? Browser TEMPLATE FILES A template is usually an HTML file. Example: Home

Welcome to Django

The template can be stored inside a templates directory. TEMPLATE RENDERING A view can render a template using render(): from django. shortcuts import render def home(request): return render(request, "home. html") Django loads the template and returns the generated HTML as the HTTP response. CONTEXT VARIABLES A view can send data to a template using a context dictionary. Example: def profile(request): context = { "name": "Student", "course": "Django", } return render( request, "profile. html", context, ) The template can display those values:

{{ name }}

{{ course }}

The double curly braces are used to display template variables. TEMPLATE TAGS Django templates also provide template tags. For example: {% if user. is_authenticated %}

Welcome back.

{% endif %} A loop can be written as: {% for course in courses %}

{{ course. title }}

{% endfor %} Template tags use {% and %}. FILTERS Django template filters can transform or format values. Example: {{ name|upper }} This displays the value in uppercase. Another example is: {{ description|truncatewords:20 }} This limits the displayed text to approximately twenty words. TEMPLATE INHERITANCE Template inheritance allows multiple pages to share a common layout. A base template can contain the overall HTML structure: {% block title %}Coding Academy{% endblock %}
Coding Academy
{% block content %} {% endblock %}
Another template can extend the base template: {% extends "base. html" %} {% block title %} Courses {% endblock %} {% block content %}

Courses

{% endblock %} This avoids duplicating the same HTML structure across many pages. BLOCKS The {% block %} tag defines areas that child templates can replace. Common blocks include: title content scripts The exact block names are chosen by the application's design. STATIC FILES Web applications usually need files that do not change for each request. Examples include: - CSS files; - JavaScript files; - images; - icons; - fonts. These are called static files. STATIC URL Django uses STATIC_URL to define the URL prefix used for static files. For example: STATIC_URL = "static/" TEMPLATE STATIC TAG A template should normally load the static template tag library: {% load static %} A CSS file can then be referenced with: An image can be referenced with: STATIC DIRECTORIES A project can contain a static directory such as: static/ css/ style. css js/ app. js images/ logo. png During development, Django can serve static files when configured appropriately. COLLECTSTATIC Before production deployment, static files are normally collected with: python manage. py collectstatic This gathers static files into the configured static files location so that they can be served efficiently in production. STATIC FILES AND WHITE NOISE Production Django applications often use a dedicated static-file serving solution. In this project, WhiteNoise is configured to help serve collected static files from the Django application. RESPONSIVE TEMPLATE DESIGN Templates should present information clearly across different screen sizes. Useful HTML elements include:
Semantic HTML can make templates easier to understand and maintain. FORMS IN TEMPLATES Django forms often appear inside templates. A POST form may look like:
{% csrf_token %} ...
The csrf_token tag provides CSRF protection for Django POST forms. TEMPLATES AND APPLICATION DESIGN Templates should focus primarily on presentation. Application logic normally belongs in Python views, models, forms, and other backend components rather than being embedded directly into HTML. A clean separation makes Django applications easier to maintain. KEY IDEAS Remember: - Templates generate HTML. - Views can pass context data to templates. - {{ variable }} displays values. - {% tag %} performs template logic. - Template inheritance reduces duplicated HTML. - {% extends %} connects a child template to a base template. - {% block %} defines replaceable sections. - Static files include CSS, JavaScript, images, and similar assets. - {% load static %} enables the static template tag. - collectstatic prepares static files for deployment. - CSRF protection should be used with Django POST forms. A strong understanding of templates and static files is important because they form the presentation layer of a Django web application.

fields.title: Models and Database Basics
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops an understanding of Django models, database tables, fields, relationships, migrations, and the ORM. Learners move from defining data structures to querying, creating, updating, deleting, and relating persistent records.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on designing data models deliberately and using the ORM to express reliable database operations while avoiding unnecessary duplication.

Django models define the data structures used by a Django application. A model is normally represented by a Python class and is connected to a database table. For example: from django. db import models class Student(models. Model): name = models. CharField(max_length=100) age = models. IntegerField() This model describes a Student object with a name and age. MODEL FIELDS Django provides many field types. Common examples include: CharField TextField IntegerField BooleanField DateField DateTimeField EmailField ForeignKey Example: class Course(models. Model): title = models. CharField(max_length=200) description = models. TextField() duration = models. IntegerField() created_at = models. DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True) Each field represents a piece of stored data. PRIMARY KEYS Django automatically provides an id field as the primary key unless another field is explicitly configured. The primary key uniquely identifies each database record. MAKING MODEL CHANGES When a model is changed, Django provides a migration workflow. First create migration files: python manage. py makemigrations Then apply them: python manage. py migrate makemigrations creates migration instructions based on model changes. migrate applies those changes to the database. THE DJANGO ORM ORM stands for Object-Relational Mapper. Django's ORM allows developers to work with database records using Python objects and querysets rather than writing SQL for every operation. For example: students = Student. objects. all() This retrieves all Student records. FILTERING RECORDS The filter() method can retrieve records matching conditions. Example: students = Student. objects. filter(age=20) Another example: students = Student. objects. filter(name="Student") GETTING ONE OBJECT The get() method can retrieve one object: student = Student. objects. get(id=1) get() should be used when one matching object is expected. CREATING OBJECTS An object can be created using: student = Student. objects. create( name="Student", age=20, ) This creates and saves the record. An alternative is: student = Student( name="Student", age=20, ) student. save() UPDATING OBJECTS An object can be modified and saved: student = Student. objects. get(id=1) student. age = 21 student. save() DELETING OBJECTS A record can be deleted with: student = Student. objects. get(id=1) student. delete() QUERYSETS A QuerySet represents a collection of database records. For example: students = Student. objects. all() A QuerySet can be filtered: students = Student. objects. filter(age__gte=18) QuerySets can also be ordered: students = Student. objects. order_by("name") COMMON LOOKUPS Django provides lookup expressions for queries. Examples: age=20 age__gte=18 age__lte=65 name__icontains="john" These allow developers to express database queries using Python syntax. RELATIONSHIPS Django supports relationships between models. A ForeignKey represents a many-to-one relationship. For example: class Course(models. Model): title = models. CharField(max_length=200) class Lesson(models. Model): course = models. ForeignKey( Course, on_delete=models. CASCADE, ) title = models. CharField(max_length=200) One course can therefore have many lessons. The related lesson records can be accessed through the relationship. DATABASE DESIGN A good database design separates related information into appropriate models. For example, an LMS might use: Course Module Lesson Activity Submission Student Relationships connect these models so that information does not have to be duplicated unnecessarily. CASCADE DELETE In the ForeignKey example: on_delete=models. CASCADE means that when the referenced Course is deleted, related Lesson records are also deleted. Other on_delete behaviors are possible, depending on the application's requirements. MODEL METHODS Models can also contain methods that operate on model instances. For example: class Student(models. Model): name = models. CharField(max_length=100) def introduce(self): return f"Hello, I am {self. name}" This allows behavior related to the model to remain close to the model data. DATABASE ADMINISTRATION Django's admin interface can use registered models to provide a convenient interface for creating, viewing, editing, and deleting records. The model therefore becomes part of several connected parts of the Django application: Model ? Migration ? Database ? ORM ? View ? Template KEY IDEAS Remember: - A Django model is a Python class representing stored data. - Model fields define the structure of that data. - makemigrations creates migration instructions. - migrate applies migrations to the database. - The Django ORM lets you work with database data using Python. - QuerySets represent collections of records. - create(), get(), filter(), save(), and delete() are common ORM operations. - ForeignKey creates relationships between models. - Good model design reduces unnecessary duplication. Understanding models and the ORM is one of the most important steps toward building real Django applications because most useful web applications need to store, retrieve, update, and relate persistent data.

fields.title: Forms and User Input
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson develops practical understanding of collecting and validating user input through Django forms and ModelForms. Learners examine GET and POST workflows, CSRF protection, cleaned data, custom validation, widgets, file uploads, and form-processing patterns.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on treating browser-submitted data as untrusted input that must be validated and handled safely on the server.

Django forms provide a structured way to collect, validate, and process user input. Forms are especially useful when a web application needs users to submit information such as: - registration details; - login credentials; - search terms; - course submissions; - profile information; - comments; - contact information. A Django form connects the browser-facing HTML form with Python validation and application logic. BASIC FORM FLOW A typical form workflow is: Browser ? GET request ? Display form ? User enters data ? POST request ? Validate submitted data ? Process cleaned data ? Save data or return errors ? Response HTML FORMS A simple HTML form may look like:
{% csrf_token %}
Django commonly uses POST requests when a form submits data that changes application state. GET requests are commonly used when retrieving or displaying information. CSRF PROTECTION Django provides Cross-Site Request Forgery protection. A POST form should normally include: {% csrf_token %} This adds a security token that Django uses to help verify that the request originates from an approved form. DJANGO FORM CLASSES Django provides a forms framework. Example: from django import forms class StudentForm(forms. Form): name = forms. CharField(max_length=100) age = forms. IntegerField() This defines a form with two fields. FORM FIELDS Common Django form fields include: CharField IntegerField EmailField BooleanField ChoiceField DateField FileField Example: class ContactForm(forms. Form): name = forms. CharField(max_length=100) email = forms. EmailField() message = forms. CharField( widget=forms. Textarea ) DISPLAYING A FORM A form can be passed from a view to a template. Example: def contact(request): form = ContactForm() return render( request, "contact. html", {"form": form}, ) The template can display the form:
{% csrf_token %} {{ form. as_p }}
FORM VALIDATION When submitted data is received, the form should be validated. Example: if request. method == "POST": form = ContactForm(request. POST) if form. is_valid(): ... else: form = ContactForm() form. is_valid() runs the configured validation rules. CLEANED DATA After successful validation, cleaned values are available through: form. cleaned_data Example: if form. is_valid(): name = form. cleaned_data["name"] age = form. cleaned_data["age"] The cleaned data has passed the form's validation process. VALIDATION ERRORS If submitted data is invalid: if not form. is_valid(): ... The form can then be rendered again so the user can see the validation errors. For example, an IntegerField will reject input that cannot be converted into an integer. CUSTOM VALIDATION A form can define custom validation logic. Example: class StudentForm(forms. Form): name = forms. CharField(max_length=100) age = forms. IntegerField() def clean_age(self): age = self. cleaned_data["age"] if age < 13: raise forms. ValidationError( "Student must be at least 13." ) return age Custom validation allows application-specific rules to be enforced. MODELFORM Django also provides ModelForm. A ModelForm creates a form based on a Django model. Example: from django import forms from . models import Student class StudentForm(forms. ModelForm): class Meta: model = Student fields = ["name", "age", "email"] This can reduce duplicated form and model definitions. SAVING A MODELFORM A valid ModelForm can save a model object: if form. is_valid(): student = form. save() The form creates and saves the associated model record. FORMS AND VIEWS A common pattern is: def student_create(request): if request. method == "POST": form = StudentForm(request. POST) if form. is_valid(): form. save() return redirect("student_list") else: form = StudentForm() return render( request, "student_form. html", {"form": form}, ) This pattern handles both displaying and processing the form. GET AND POST The two common request methods have different roles. GET: Usually retrieves information or displays a form. POST: Usually submits data for processing. For example: GET /students/create/ displays the form POST /students/create/ processes the submitted form FORM WIDGETS Widgets control how fields are represented in HTML. For example: forms. Textarea forms. PasswordInput forms. Select forms. DateInput Example: message = forms. CharField( widget=forms. Textarea ) This tells Django to render the field as a textarea. CHOICE FIELDS A form can offer predefined choices. Example: class CourseForm(forms. Form): level = forms. ChoiceField( choices=[ ("beginner", "Beginner"), ("intermediate", "Intermediate"), ("advanced", "Advanced"), ] ) This helps control the values users can submit. FILE UPLOADS Django forms can also handle file uploads using FileField. A file upload form commonly uses:
The uploaded files are then available through the request's FILES data and can be passed to the form. FORMS AND SECURITY Forms should validate user input rather than trusting the browser. Important practices include: - validate submitted data; - use CSRF protection for POST forms; - avoid trusting hidden fields; - enforce authorization in server-side code; - validate uploaded files; - sanitize or safely render user-provided content. FORMS IN AN LMS A learning platform can use forms for: - student registration; - profile editing; - assignment submission; - instructor feedback; - course creation; - quiz responses; - search; - filtering. For example, an instructor grading form might collect a score and feedback, validate those values, and then update a Submission model. KEY IDEAS Remember: - Django forms collect and validate user input. - GET commonly displays forms. - POST commonly processes submitted data. - {% csrf_token %} protects POST forms against CSRF attacks. - form. is_valid() runs validation. - form. cleaned_data contains validated values. - ModelForm connects forms directly to models. - Custom validation can enforce application-specific rules. - Widgets control how form fields are rendered. - Server-side validation is essential even when browser validation exists. Understanding forms is an important step toward building interactive Django applications because forms connect user input to validated backend logic.

fields.title: Authentication and Authorization
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson examines identity and access control in Django. Learners explore user accounts, password handling, sessions, authentication helpers, permissions, groups, staff users, ownership checks, and role-based access.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on designing access-control policies that remain enforceable even when users bypass the visible frontend and request protected resources directly.

Django includes a built-in authentication system for identifying users and controlling access to application features. Authentication answers: "Who is this user?" Authorization answers: "What is this user allowed to do?" These are related but different concepts. DJANGO USERS Django provides a User model that can store information such as: - username; - password; - email address; - first name; - last name; - active status; - staff status; - superuser status. Passwords should never be stored as plain text. Django provides password hashing and authentication helpers so applications do not need to manage password storage manually. CREATING USERS Users can be created through application forms, management commands, the Django admin, or Python code. For example: from django. contrib. auth import get_user_model User = get_user_model() user = User. objects. create_user( username="student", password="secure-password", ) The create_user() helper handles password hashing correctly. LOGGING USERS IN Django provides authentication helpers. A common login flow uses authenticate() and login(): from django. contrib. auth import authenticate, login user = authenticate( username=username, password=password, ) if user is not None: login(request, user) authenticate() checks the submitted credentials. login() associates the authenticated user with the current session. LOGGING USERS OUT A user can be logged out with: from django. contrib. auth import logout logout(request) This removes the authenticated user's session information. REQUEST. USER Django makes the current user available through: request. user A view can check whether the user is authenticated: if request. user. is_authenticated: ... This is useful when a page should behave differently for signed-in and anonymous visitors. LOGIN_REQUIRED Django provides the login_required decorator. Example: from django. contrib. auth. decorators import login_required @login_required def dashboard(request): ... If an anonymous user tries to access this view, Django redirects the user to the configured login page. LOGIN REQUIRED AND SENSITIVE ACTIONS Pages that access private information or allow users to change application data should normally enforce authentication. Examples include: - student dashboards; - profile pages; - submission pages; - instructor tools; - account settings. STAFF USERS Django users can have an is_staff flag. Staff users can be allowed to access the Django administration interface. However, being authenticated is not the same as being authorized to perform every action. SUPERUSERS A superuser has full permissions in Django's standard administration system. A superuser can normally be created with: python manage. py createsuperuser PERMISSIONS Django provides a permissions system for controlling access to actions. Permissions can be assigned to users or groups. A permission can represent an operation such as adding, changing, deleting, or viewing a model. For example, an application might allow: Students: - view courses; - submit activities; - view their own progress. Instructors: - review submissions; - provide grades; - manage course content. Administrators: - manage users; - manage system data; - access administrative tools. GROUPS Django groups can organize users who share permissions. For example: Students Instructors Administrators A group can receive permissions that apply to its members. CHECKING PERMISSIONS A view can check whether a user has a permission: if request. user. has_perm("academy. change_course"): ... Authorization checks should happen on the server. Do not rely only on hiding buttons or links in HTML because a user could attempt to access the URL directly. OBJECT-LEVEL ACCESS Some applications need to check ownership as well as general permissions. For example, a student should normally be allowed to see their own submission, but not another student's private submission. A view can enforce this by querying an object with the authenticated user: submission = get_object_or_404( Submission, id=submission_id, student=request. user, ) This ensures the object belongs to the current user. INSTRUCTOR ACCESS Instructor pages may require more than authentication. For example: @login_required def instructor_dashboard(request): if not request. user. is_staff: return redirect("home") ... The exact authorization strategy should match the application's roles and permission requirements. AUTHENTICATION VS AUTHORIZATION Remember the difference: Authentication: Identifies the user. Authorization: Determines what the identified user may access or modify. A user may be authenticated but still not have permission to access a particular resource. SESSION AUTHENTICATION Django's web authentication system commonly uses sessions. After login, Django maintains session information so that subsequent requests can identify the authenticated user. This allows pages to use: request. user without requiring the user to enter credentials for every request. SECURITY PRINCIPLES Important authentication and authorization practices include: - use Django's password hashing; - never store plain-text passwords; - protect sensitive views with authentication checks; - enforce authorization on the server; - verify ownership of private objects; - use HTTPS in production; - protect POST requests with CSRF protection; - avoid exposing sensitive information in URLs or templates; - keep session and authentication configuration secure. API AUTHENTICATION Django REST Framework can use authentication mechanisms such as token authentication. This is different from normal browser session authentication, although both serve the broader purpose of identifying the caller. An API endpoint can require authentication with DRF permissions such as: from rest_framework. permissions import IsAuthenticated An API request can then be restricted to authenticated clients. ROLE-BASED LMS EXAMPLE A coding-learning platform may implement: Student ??? browse courses ??? enroll ??? submit activities ??? view personal progress Instructor ??? manage learning content ??? review submissions ??? provide assessment Administrator ??? manage users ??? manage application data ??? access administration tools The exact implementation should use server-side permission checks rather than depending only on the visible interface. KEY IDEAS Remember: - Authentication identifies a user. - Authorization controls access. - request. user represents the current user. - @login_required protects views from anonymous access. - is_staff and superuser status provide administrative capabilities. - Django permissions and groups provide finer-grained access control. - Object-level ownership checks protect private records. - Browser sessions and API tokens are different authentication mechanisms. - Security checks must be enforced on the server. Authentication and authorization are essential for a real Django application because user identity and access control must be enforced consistently across pages, forms, APIs, and administrative tools.

fields.title: Django Admin and Application Management
fields.content:
Lesson overview. This lesson examines Django's administrative interface as an internal management capability rather than a substitute for the public application interface. Learners explore model registration, ModelAdmin customisation, searching, filtering, read-only fields, inlines, permissions, and administrative security.

Professional focus. The professional focus is on using administrative tooling responsibly while maintaining clear boundaries between operational management and the learner-facing application.

Django includes an administrative interface that allows authorized users to manage application data through a web browser. The Django admin is especially useful for development, content management, and internal administration. WHAT IS DJANGO ADMIN? Django Admin provides a web-based interface for managing registered models. For example, an LMS administrator may use the admin interface to manage: - users; - courses; - modules; - lessons; - activities; - submissions. Instead of writing database queries manually, an authorized administrator can create, view, update, and delete records through the admin interface. CREATING AN ADMIN USER A user with administrator access can be created with: python manage. py createsuperuser Django asks for the required account information and password. The resulting superuser can normally sign in to: /admin/ depending on the project's URL configuration. REGISTERING A MODEL A model must be registered with the admin interface before it can normally appear there. For example: from django. contrib import admin from . models import Student admin. site. register(Student) After registration, Student records can be managed through the admin site. MODELADMIN Django allows developers to customize how a model appears in the admin. Example: @admin. register(Student) class StudentAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): list_display = ("name", "age", "email") This controls which fields are displayed in the list view. LIST DISPLAY list_display defines columns shown in the model's admin list. Example: class CourseAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): list_display = ( "title", "instructor", "created_at", ) This makes important information visible without opening every object. SEARCH The search_fields option enables searching. Example: class CourseAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): search_fields = ( "title", "description", ) An administrator can then search for matching course records. FILTERS The list_filter option adds filtering controls. Example: class CourseAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): list_filter = ( "level", "created_at", ) Filters are useful when an administrator needs to narrow a large list of records. ORDERING ModelAdmin can control default ordering. Example: class CourseAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): ordering = ("title",) The admin list will then be ordered by title. READONLY FIELDS Some fields should be displayed but not edited manually. Example: class CourseAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): readonly_fields = ("created_at",) This can protect automatically generated information. FIELDSETS Django admin allows related fields to be grouped visually. For larger models, fieldsets can make edit pages easier to understand. Example: class StudentAdmin(admin. ModelAdmin): fieldsets = ( ("Identity", { "fields": ("name", "email"), }), ("Details", { "fields": ("age",), }), ) AUTOMATIC ADMIN FORMS The Django admin automatically generates forms for registered models. It applies model field definitions and many model validation rules when creating and editing records. INLINE ADMIN Related models can sometimes be edited together using inline admin classes. For example, an administrator managing a Course might want to see related Lesson records on the same page. A simplified example is: class LessonInline(admin. TabularInline): model = Lesson Then the inline can be attached to a CourseAdmin. This can make management of related records more efficient. ADMIN PERMISSIONS The admin interface is intended for authorized users. Django distinguishes user capabilities using permissions and staff status. A staff user can access the admin site when configured and authorized to do so. Object permissions such as add, change, delete, and view can also be controlled. SECURITY AND DJANGO ADMIN The admin interface should not be treated as a public user interface. Important practices include: - use strong passwords; - restrict access to authorized staff; - use HTTPS in production; - protect administrative accounts; - review permissions; - avoid giving unnecessary privileges; - keep Django and dependencies updated; - monitor administrative access. ADMIN VS APPLICATION UI The Django admin is excellent for internal management, but it is not always the best interface for students or public users. For example: Student-facing pages: - course browsing; - lessons; - activities; - progress; - submissions. Administrative pages: - managing users; - editing course content; - reviewing data; - maintaining system records. A production application may use both the Django admin and custom application interfaces. DJANGO ADMIN WORKFLOW A typical workflow is: 1. Define a model. 2. Register the model in admin. py. 3. Customize ModelAdmin if needed. 4. Create an authorized staff account. 5. Sign in to /admin/. 6. Create or modify records. 7. Verify the application behavior. DJANGO ADMIN IN AN LMS In a learning platform, administrators might use Django Admin to inspect: Course ↓ Module ↓ Lesson ↓ Activity ↓ Submission This makes it possible to maintain learning content and review application data without directly editing database tables. COMMON MODELADMIN OPTIONS Useful ModelAdmin options include: list_display search_fields list_filter ordering readonly_fields fieldsets inlines These options allow the admin interface to become much more useful for managing real application data. KEY IDEAS Remember: - Django Admin provides a browser-based administrative interface. - Models must be registered before they normally appear in admin. - ModelAdmin customizes the admin experience. - list_display controls list columns. - search_fields adds searching. - list_filter adds filtering. - readonly_fields can protect generated data. - inlines can manage related objects together. - Admin access should be restricted to authorized users. Django Admin is an important productivity tool because it provides a powerful internal interface for managing application data while allowing the public-facing application to use its own custom user experience.

fields.title: Introduction to APIs and REST
fields.content:
Introduction to APIs and REST

Modern software systems rarely operate as isolated applications. Web frontends, mobile applications, desktop clients, automated services, and third-party integrations often need to exchange information with a backend system. An Application Programming Interface, or API, provides a structured boundary through which these systems communicate.

In a technology-learning platform, the frontend may request a public course catalogue, retrieve the details of a particular course, submit an assignment, record completion of a learning activity, or retrieve authenticated learner progress. Each interaction can be represented through a predictable HTTP endpoint and a clearly defined response.

API Request and Response

A typical interaction begins with a client constructing an HTTP request. The request reaches a URL endpoint, where backend application logic may authenticate the caller, validate the request, retrieve or modify database records, apply business rules, and construct the resulting response. 

Client
  |
HTTP request
  |
URL endpoint
  |
Backend view
  |
Application logic / database
  |
HTTP response
  |
Client

RESTful Resource Design

REST stands for Representational State Transfer. It is an architectural style commonly associated with web APIs. A REST-oriented design generally treats important application concepts as resources. A learning platform may expose courses, modules, lessons, activities, submissions, users, notifications, and progress as distinct resources.

The objective is to create an interface whose structure is understandable, predictable, and consistent. HTTP methods communicate the intended operation: GET commonly retrieves information, POST creates or initiates an operation, PUT replaces a representation, PATCH partially updates one, and DELETE removes a resource.

HTTP Status Codes and JSON

HTTP status codes communicate the outcome of an operation. Successful requests generally use the 2xx range, client-side problems use the 4xx range, and unexpected server failures use the 5xx range. JSON is widely used to represent structured API data because it is portable and well supported by modern programming environments.

Authentication and Authorization

Authentication establishes the identity associated with a request, while authorization determines what that identity is permitted to do. This distinction is fundamental when protecting learner progress, submissions, instructor grading operations, or administrative functions.

fields.title: DRF Project Setup and Configuration
fields.content:
DRF Project Setup and Configuration

Before an API can expose meaningful application resources, Django REST Framework must be integrated correctly with the Django project. This foundation influences request handling, serialization, authentication, permissions, rendering, testing, and other framework behaviour.

Installing DRF

Django REST Framework is installed as a Python dependency. A typical installation uses the package manager: 

pip install djangorestframework

In a professional application, the dependency should also be recorded in the project's requirements or dependency-management system so that development, testing, and production environments remain consistent.

Project Integration

The framework is normally added to INSTALLED_APPS so that Django loads it as part of the project configuration. API URL patterns then connect client requests to DRF views. For a class-based view, as_view() converts the view class into a callable that Django's URL resolver can invoke.

Working with Request Data

DRF exposes parsed request-body information through request. data and query-string parameters through request. query_params. These interfaces provide a clean boundary between raw HTTP input and application logic.

Global REST Framework Settings

The REST_FRAMEWORK configuration can establish defaults for authentication, permissions, pagination, rendering, throttling, and other behaviour. Such defaults should be chosen deliberately because they influence the baseline behaviour of API endpoints throughout the project.

fields.title: Serializers and Data Validation
fields.content:
Serializers and Data Validation

Serializers establish a controlled boundary between Django's internal Python objects and the structured representations exchanged with API clients. They are central to both the representation of server-side data and the validation of information received from external systems.

Serialization

A Django model instance exists internally as a Python object, while an API client generally expects structured information such as JSON. A serializer can transform the internal object into a representation suitable for an HTTP response.

Deserialization

The reverse process occurs when a client submits data. DRF can parse the incoming representation and pass it through a serializer so that the application can validate the information before trusting it or using it to create or update database records. 

request. data
    |
serializer
    |
is_valid()
    |
validated_data
    |
save()

ModelSerializer

ModelSerializer provides a concise way to derive serializer fields from a Django model. It reduces repetitive declarations while still allowing the developer to control read-only fields, relationships, defaults, and custom validation rules.

The Server as the Final Validation Boundary

Client-side validation improves user experience, but it must never be treated as the final authority. A modified client, automated script, or alternative application can bypass frontend validation completely. The backend must therefore enforce the rules that protect application integrity.

It is also important to distinguish serializer. data from serializer. validated_data. The first represents serialized output, while the second contains values produced after successful validation of incoming input.

fields.title: Function-Based API Views
fields.content:
Function-Based API Views

Django REST Framework supports function-based API views through the @api_view decorator. This approach provides a concise way to understand the essential request-response lifecycle before introducing more structured class-based abstractions. 

from rest_framework. decorators import api_view
from rest_framework. response import Response

@api_view(["GET"])
def course_list(request):
    return Response({
        "message": "Course list"
    })

HTTP Method Control

The decorator specifies which HTTP methods the function accepts. An endpoint may support more than one method where the resource requires different operations, and request. method can be inspected when distinct behaviours must be implemented.

Request and Response Data

Request-body information is available through request. data, while query-string information is available through request. query_params. The DRF Response class provides a consistent mechanism for returning structured information and appropriate HTTP status codes.

Designing Clear Endpoints

Function-based views can be particularly expressive for small or specialised operations. As an application grows, however, repeated patterns may justify class-based or generic abstractions that improve structure and reuse. Regardless of the chosen style, validation, permissions, and predictable responses remain essential responsibilities.

fields.title: Class-Based API Views and Generic Views
fields.content:
Class-Based API Views and Generic Views

As API systems become larger, developers often benefit from organising related request behaviours inside classes. Django REST Framework's class-based views provide structure, reuse, and a clear mapping between HTTP methods and application operations.

APIView

APIView allows methods such as get(), post(), put(), patch(), and delete() to express the operations supported by an endpoint. The URL configuration connects the class to Django's request lifecycle through as_view().

Generic Views

Generic views provide reusable implementations for conventional API patterns. Examples include ListAPIView, CreateAPIView, ListCreateAPIView, and RetrieveUpdateDestroyAPIView. These abstractions commonly work with a queryset and serializer_class.

Methods such as get_queryset() and perform_create() can be customised when application-specific behaviour is required. This allows developers to retain framework-provided behaviour while introducing precise business rules where necessary.

Choosing an Appropriate Abstraction

APIView is often appropriate when an endpoint contains specialised processing that does not correspond neatly to standard CRUD behaviour. Generic views are particularly useful when the resource follows established patterns and the developer can benefit from consistency and reduced duplication.

fields.title: ViewSets and Routers
fields.content:
ViewSets and Routers

Django REST Framework ViewSets provide a compact way to group related operations around a resource. They are especially useful when a resource supports conventional operations such as listing, creating, retrieving, updating, and deleting records.

Standard ViewSet Actions

Common actions include list, create, retrieve, update, partial_update, and destroy. ModelViewSet builds upon this pattern and can supply standard CRUD behaviour when given a queryset and serializer.

Routers

Routers connect ViewSets to URL patterns automatically. A DefaultRouter can register a resource and derive predictable routes for standard operations. This reduces repetitive URL configuration and encourages a consistent API surface.

Custom Actions

Not every application operation is naturally expressed as CRUD. The @action decorator permits domain-specific operations to be associated with a resource. A course progress operation, for example, can be modelled as specialised behaviour associated with a particular course.

Routers provide convenience, not automatic security. Developers must still define authentication, permissions, ownership, and role-specific rules.

fields.title: Authentication and Permissions
fields.content:
Authentication and Permissions

A secure API must determine both the identity of the caller and the authority associated with that identity. Django REST Framework separates these responsibilities through authentication and permission mechanisms.

Authentication

Authentication answers the question: who is making this request? DRF supports multiple authentication strategies, including token-based and session-based mechanisms. The selected authentication class determines how credentials are interpreted and how the request becomes associated with a Django user.

Permissions and Authorization

Permissions answer a different question: is this caller allowed to perform the requested operation? An authenticated user can therefore still be denied access because the user's role, ownership, or other authorization conditions do not satisfy the endpoint's policy. 

from rest_framework. permissions import IsAuthenticated

class ProgressAPIView(APIView):
    permission_classes = [IsAuthenticated]

Ownership and Least Privilege

A learner should normally be able to access private progress and submissions belonging to that learner, while an instructor may require broader privileges for assessment and grading tasks. Least privilege means granting only the access genuinely required for a responsibility.

This approach reduces unnecessary exposure and limits the consequences of configuration mistakes or compromised credentials.

fields.title: API Testing and Production Practices
fields.content:
API Testing and Production Practices

An API should not be considered complete merely because its endpoints return successful responses during manual testing. Production-quality services must also behave predictably when input is invalid, authentication is missing, permissions are insufficient, resources do not exist, or unexpected failures occur.

Automated API Testing

Django REST Framework provides testing utilities such as APIClient and APITestCase for exercising API behaviour programmatically. A mature test suite should cover both successful operations and important failure conditions, including validation, authentication, authorization, and business rules.

Observability and Documentation

Operational confidence also depends on useful logging, appropriate observability, clear API documentation, predictable status codes, and secure configuration. These practices make the service easier to maintain and debug after deployment.

Production Verification

After deployment, representative public and protected endpoints should be tested in the actual environment. Authentication flows, important business operations, and meaningful failure cases should be verified rather than assumed to work simply because deployment completed successfully.

Testing and operational discipline transform an API from a collection of working endpoints into a dependable service that can evolve with confidence.

fields.title: Python Introduction Exercise
fields.instructions:
Write a simple Python program that displays the following message:

Welcome to Python Programming!

Run your program and make sure the message is displayed correctly.

fields.title: Python Basics Reading
fields.instructions: Read the lesson carefully and identify three important concepts you have learned about Python.

fields.title: Variables Practice
fields.instructions: Create a Python program that stores your name, age, and height in variables. Use appropriate data types for each value, then print all three values.

fields.title: Data Types Exercise
fields.instructions: Create four Python variables demonstrating the following data types: integer, float, string, and Boolean. Print each variable and its value.

fields.title: Variables and Data Types Reading
fields.instructions: Read the lesson carefully. Identify the four basic Python data types discussed in this lesson and explain briefly what each type is used for.

fields.title: Using print()
fields.instructions:
Write a Python program that uses print() to display the following three lines:

Welcome to Python Programming!
I am learning Python.
Python is fun!

Run your program and verify that all three lines are displayed correctly.

fields.title: Getting User Input
fields.instructions:
Write a Python program that asks the user to enter their name and age.

Store the name in a variable called name and the age in a variable called age.

Display the information using print().

Example interaction:

Enter your name: Victor
Enter your age: 25

Your name is Victor
Your age is 25

Remember to convert the age to an integer using int().

fields.title: Input and Output Challenge
fields.instructions:
Create a Python program that asks the user for:

1. Their name
2. Their age
3. Their height in metres

Convert the age to an integer and the height to a floating-point number.

Then display all the information.

Your program should demonstrate the use of:

input()
int()
float()
print()

Test your program with different values.

fields.title: Input and Output Review
fields.instructions:
Review the lesson and explain the purpose of:

1. print()
2. input()
3. int()
4. float()

Also explain why input() values sometimes need to be converted before performing mathematical operations.

fields.title: Loops Reading
For Loop Practice
fields.instructions:
Write a Python program using a for loop.

Your program must:
1. Use range() to count from 1 to 5.
2. Print each number on a separate line.

Expected output:

1
2
3
4
5

Run your code first, then submit it when the output is correct.

fields.title: Loop Challenge
fields.instructions:
Write a Python program that uses a for loop to print all even numbers
from 1 through 10.

Expected output:

2
4
6
8
10

Requirements:
- Use a for loop.
- Use range().
- Use a conditional check to identify even numbers.

Run your program and submit the completed solution for assessment.

fields.title: Functions Reading
Function Practice
fields.instructions:
Write a Python function called greet that accepts a name parameter and
prints:

Hello, <name>!

Call the function using the name "Student".

Expected output:

Hello, Student!

Run your code and submit it when the output is correct.

fields.title: Return Value Challenge
fields.instructions:
Write a function called add_numbers that accepts two numbers and returns
